items.title: 1.10 Variation in oxidation number in oxides and chlorides

source_refs.note: Topic 1.10, printed page 18: oxidation numbers in period 3 oxides and chlorides and Table 1.2. The printed table gives S in SCl2 as -2; it is recorded as printed.

blocks.title: Oxidation number
blocks.text: The oxidation number, or oxidation state, of an atom is the formal charge on that atom in a molecule or ion. In ionic compounds it is the charge that appears on the ion.

For an element of period 3, the oxidation number in its oxide or chloride corresponds to the number of electrons used for bonding and is always positive, because oxygen and chlorine are more electronegative than any of these elements. It matches the group number, reflecting the total number of valence electrons. In the oxides the oxidation number rises from +1 in sodium to +6 in sulfur; in the chlorides from +1 in sodium to +5 in phosphorus. Phosphorus and sulfur show several oxidation numbers because they can expand their octet by exciting electrons into empty 3d orbitals: in SO2 sulfur is +4 because only four electrons are used for bonding, while in SO3 it is +6 because all six are used.

blocks.prompt: Calculate the oxidation number of sulfur in SO2 and SO3, and explain why some p block elements show variable oxidation states.
blocks.explanation: Oxygen is -2 each. In SO2, x + 2(-2) = 0 gives x = +4; in SO3, x + 3(-2) = 0 gives x = +6. Phosphorus and sulfur can promote electrons into their empty 3d orbitals and so use more of their valence electrons for bonding, giving +3 or +5 for phosphorus and +4 or +6 for sulfur.

items: Oxidation number is the formal charge on an atom in a molecule or ion; in period 3 oxides and chlorides it is positive and equals the electrons used for bonding, matching the group number: +1 (Na) to +6 (S) in oxides, +1 to +5 (P) in chlorides.
P and S show several values by expanding the octet into 3d orbitals: SO2 +4, SO3 +6.
